S1.title: Python Lecture Notes
S1.text: 1. Variables and Data Types A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory. In Python you create a variable by assignment, for example age = 21. Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so the same name can later refer to a string. The core built-in types are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), bool (True or False) and NoneType (the single value None, meaning "no value"). The function type(x) reports the type of x. Conversion functions such as int("42"), float("3.5") and str(10) create new values of another type; int("abc") raises a ValueError. Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero, so "python"[0] is "p", and negative indexes count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).

You raise an exception yourself with raise ValueError("age must be positive"). Custom exceptions are created by subclassing Exception. Common error messages: IndentationError means inconsistent indentation, NameError means a name was used before assignment, and IndexError means a list index was out of range.

S3.title: Ml Reference Notes
S3.text: Feature: an input variable used by a model, for example a person's age. Label or target: the value the model should predict. Hyperparameter: a setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate, tree depth or number of neighbors k. Parameter: a value learned during training, such as the weights of linear regression. Epoch: one full pass through the training data. Batch size: the number of examples used for one gradient update. Learning rate: the step size of gradient descent. Regularization: a penalty that discourages overly complex models. L2 (ridge) shrinks weights; L1 (lasso) can set weights to zero. Overfitting: low training error but high validation error because the model memorized noise. Underfitting: high error on both training and validation data because the model is too simple. Bias: error from wrong or overly simple assumptions.

Since Python 3.7 dictionaries preserve insertion order. Dictionary comprehensions such as {w: len(w) for w in words} are common. Copying matters: b = a makes both names refer to the same list, while b = a.copy() creates a shallow copy. A shallow copy still shares nested objects; copy.deepcopy copies them too.

S5.title: Python Lecture Notes
S5.text: 4. Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries A list is an ordered, mutable sequence: nums = [3, 1, 2]. Common methods are append(x) to add at the end, insert(i, x), remove(x), pop() to remove and return the last item, and sort() to sort in place. The built-in sorted(nums) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. List comprehensions build lists concisely: [n * n for n in nums if n > 1]. A tuple is an ordered but immutable sequence, written (1, 2). Tuples are used for fixed records and can be dictionary keys because they are hashable. A set stores unique, unordered elements and supports fast membership tests plus union (|), intersection (&) and difference (-). A dictionary maps keys to values: ages = {"Ali": 20, "Mona": 22}.
